teaser: The busiest sculptor in America made her for free, to spin on top of a tower.

lesson.text: In 1891 Augustus Saint-Gaudens had more work than one man could finish. At forty-three he was the most wanted sculptor in the United States, with monuments to generals and presidents on order and a Civil War memorial for Boston already years overdue. So what he did next made little business sense: he took on a huge extra job and asked no fee for it.

The job was for a friend. The architect Stanford White was building Madison Square Garden in New York, a pleasure palace with a tower more than 300 feet high, about 90 meters. He wanted something dazzling on the very top. Saint-Gaudens proposed Diana, Roman goddess of the hunt and of the moon, as a weathervane: a figure that swings to show which way the wind blows.

The first Diana was 18 feet tall (5.5 meters) and weighed about 1,800 pounds. Once she was up, both friends saw that she was far too big for the tower. They took her down at their own expense and made a second one, 13 feet tall, which went up in 1893.

A weathervane sets a strange problem for a sculptor. The figure must turn freely on one point, so everything rests on a single foot. It has to be read from the street, hundreds of feet below, as a dark shape against the sky. Saint-Gaudens answered with a few clean lines, and they survive in the small gilded version you see here.
Strip the figure down to its structure.

lines.label: The axis
lines.text: From the toe on the ball up through hip and head, the body is one tall, slightly leaning column. All the weight comes down on a spot the size of a coin.

lines.label: The arrow
lines.text: The outstretched arm, the arrow and the drawn-back elbow make a level bar across the top. On the tower, this bar pointed into the wind.

lines.label: The counterweight
lines.text: The free leg trails behind. It balances the bow in front, the way a tightrope walker's pole keeps a body steady.

lesson.text: Those three lines make a figure that seems to weigh nothing. She does not stride or crouch like a hunter. She hovers, calm, at the moment before release. Saint-Gaudens had trained in Paris and Rome, and you can feel classical statues behind her, but the slim, athletic body belongs to his own time.

Diana is the only female nude Saint-Gaudens ever made, and she caused trouble. Moral campaigners protested against a naked woman standing over the city. The first version had a loose scarf of metal drapery, meant to catch the wind like a rudder. It soon blew away.

The tower figure was hammered from thin sheets of copper and covered in gold leaf, so she flashed in the sun and glowed under electric lights at night. New Yorkers adored her. Saint-Gaudens saw a chance to earn something from his free gift after all, and began selling reduced bronze casts for homes. The one in this photograph is of that kind.

lesson.title: Made for a tabletop
lesson.text: A reduction lets you see up close what was once 300 feet overhead.

spots.title: Bow, arrow, string
spots.text: The bow is fully drawn, with the string pulled back to her cheek. Her head, with its hair tied up in a knot, turns in profile to sight along the arrow.

spots.title: One toe, one ball
spots.text: Only the tip of her left foot touches the sphere. The ball hints at the moon, Diana's planet, and recalls the pivot on which the big statue turned.

lesson.text: Madison Square Garden was torn down in 1925, and Diana spent seven years in storage. In 1932 the second version was given to the Philadelphia Museum of Art, where she still stands at the top of the main staircase. The first version had gone to the 1893 Chicago World's Fair and was later lost.
Diana shows how a practical object, a wind indicator, can drive artistic choices. The need to balance on one point and to read clearly from far away produced the lightness that made her famous.

The story of the two friends ended under her feet. In June 1906 Stanford White was shot dead by a jealous millionaire during a show at the rooftop theater of Madison Square Garden, directly below the statue. Saint-Gaudens, already gravely ill, died the next summer.

quiz.question: What was Diana originally made to be?
options: A weathervane on top of a tower
quiz.explanation: She crowned Madison Square Garden and turned with the wind.

quiz.question: What did Saint-Gaudens charge for the statue?
options: Nothing, he made it for his friend Stanford White
The highest fee of his career
quiz.explanation: He took no fee, though he was overloaded with paid commissions.

quiz.question: Why was the first version replaced?
options: It was too big for the tower
quiz.explanation: At 18 feet she was out of scale, so a 13-foot version replaced her in 1893.

quiz.question: What balances the bow in the composition?
quiz.explanation: The free leg stretches back as a counterweight.

quiz.question: Where is the second tower version today?
quiz.explanation: It was given to Philadelphia in 1932 after the Garden was demolished.

facts.text: The tower statue was carved from a single block of marble.
facts.explanation: It was hammered from thin sheets of copper and gilded.

facts.text: Diana is the only female nude Saint-Gaudens made.
facts.explanation: His other works are portraits, monuments and draped figures.

facts.text: Saint-Gaudens sold smaller bronze versions of Diana for private homes.
facts.explanation: Her popularity let him earn money from reductions like the one shown.
